scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is acting appropriately or not. Let me break it down step by step. First, the situation: a 31-year-old man works in an office with a 26-year-old woman. They sit together and talk a lot to pass the time. She starts inviting him out for drinks on Fridays, as friends. He makes excuses for a couple of weeks, then she asks if he dislikes her. He tells her he doesn't do friendships with women because he feels territorial when they talk to other guys or get attention, which makes him agitated. He says he doesn't act on it but hates the feeling, so he avoids it. She suggests he see a psychologist, which he refuses. Since then, their conversations have become work-related only. He's wondering if he should have lied instead of being honest. He also mentions that he feels the same way at work but can't avoid it because it's work. He doesn't want to put himself through unnecessary discomfort outside of work. He knows his feelings aren't correct but can't help it. He told a friend, who thinks he might have been controlling with past girlfriends, but he insists that's not the case. He says if the woman is his, he's okay with her talking to others because he knows she's his. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for him to tell her he doesn't do friendships with women because of these feelings? AITA (Am I the Asshole)? Let me consider the different aspects. 1. **Honesty vs. Deception**: He chose to be honest about his feelings, which is generally seen as a positive trait. However, honesty can sometimes be hurtful or lead to unintended consequences, like the woman suggesting he see a psychologist. On the other hand, lying to avoid discomfort might seem easier but could lead to problems down the line if the truth comes out. 2. **Impact on the Relationship**: By telling her, he's potentially damaged their working relationship, which has become more formal and less friendly. This could affect their ability to work together comfortably. However, he might feel better knowing he was truthful, even if it caused some distance. 3. **His Feelings and Behavior**: He describes feeling territorial and agitated when she interacts with other men, which he knows isn't correct but can't help. This seems like an insecurity or jealousy issue. He mentions that if she were his girlfriend, he wouldn't mind, which suggests that his feelings are more about possessiveness than genuine friendship. 4. **Workplace Dynamics**: It's important to maintain a professional environment. His honesty might have crossed a line into making the woman uncomfortable or affecting their workplace interactions. It's one thing to have personal feelings, but expressing them in a work setting can be problematic. 5. **Psychological Perspective**: The woman suggested he see a psychologist, which indicates that his behavior might be seen as concerning. His refusal to seek help, while understandable, might mean he's not addressing the root of his issues, which could affect his personal and professional relationships. 6. **Control and Past Relationships**: His friend thinks he might have been controlling in past relationships, which he denies. However, his current behavior could be interpreted as controlling, especially if he's trying to limit her interactions with others to avoid his discomfort. 7. **His Own Happiness vs. Others':** He prioritizes his own comfort by avoiding friendships with women, which might be fair, but it also affects others. The woman might have been looking forward to spending time with him, and his refusal could make her feel rejected or uncomfortable. Considering all these points, it seems like his honesty, while truthful, might have been unnecessary and hurtful. He could have found a way to decline her invitations without revealing such personal and potentially off-putting feelings. His behavior might be seen as controlling or insecure, which could make him the asshole in this situation.
